text.p: Chinese authorities executed eight people in the restive northwestern Moslem region of Xinjiang on Thursday for carrying out bombings, murders and robberies that left 18 people dead, Xinhua news agency said.
The executions brought to 12 the number of Moslems put to death since April for anti-Chinese unrest.

Mahmut Abdurahman, Jilil Bilali and six others were put to death in the regional capital of Urumqi after the Xinjiang Higher People's Court rejected their appeals and upheld death sentences handed down by a lower court.
The group committed violent "terrorist" crimes "by extremely cruel and criminal means", Xinhua quoted the court verdict as saying.

After an open trial, the court ruled that the gang "seriously endangered the life and property of the people, the way in which the crimes were committed was absolutely vile and the consequences extremely grave", Xinhua said.
They were found guilty of planting home-made bombs on public buses which blew up within minutes of each other in Urumqi on February 25, killing nine people and injuring 58 others.
The attacks coincided with funeral rites in Beijing for paramount leader Deng Xiaoping who died in February aged 92. The group planted two other bombs which did not explode.
Exiled separatists of the ethnic Uighur minority have claimed responsibility for the assaults and vowed to stage more until they gain freedom for their homeland.
Turkish-speaking Uighur militant want to set up an independent East Turkestan in Xinjiang.
Armed with three pistols and knives, six death-row convicts murdered and robbed nine taxi drivers, shop owners and pedestrians between December 18, 1996 and February 20, 1997, Xinhua said.
The court gave four co-defendants sentences of up to suspended death sentence, Xinhua said. Suspended death sentences are usually commuted to life imprisonment.
Last month, a Moslem was executed for bombing a military jeep last year.
In April, Chinese authorities executed three rioters and opened fire on a mob killing two men who tried to rescue the death-row convicts.
Riots in Yining in February this year had began as demonstrations for Xinjiang independence and turned violent, leaving nine people dead and 198 injured.
Xinjiang has been shaken since last year by frequent bombings as well as assassination attempts on officials and Moslem leaders seen as favouring Beijing.
China's leaders have said the battle against separatism would continue to top the government's agenda in Xinjiang.
Authorities have intensified a crackdown on separatists as well as on underground religious activity in Xinjiang, which borders Afghanistan, Pakistan and three mostly Central Asian states.
